Checking in with Chicken

28 October 20264 minute read721 words

We describe Exciting as a prototyping studio, but there isn’t much on this site that shows what that looks like these days. So here’s an example: Chicken, a small app I built at Good Enough in 2023 to help a remote team feel a bit more like a team. The name is a playful anagram of “check-in”.

The question

Good Enough was a fully remote team, spread across a handful of time zones. Remote work has a lot going for it, but you lose the small, ambient things a shared office gives you for free: glancing up from your desk and seeing who’s around, who’s heads-down, and roughly what everyone is up to. We’d been thinking about what holds a remote team together, and Chicken was a way to poke at that question with real software instead of more talking.

Slack and friends do have a “status” and a “presence”, but there’s nowhere to see everyone’s at once, and presence is mostly just “here” or “away”. So most people ignore them, or only use them for “lunch” and “done for the day”.

What it does

Very little, on purpose. Chicken is a single list: the people on your team, whether they’re around, and a short note about what they’re doing. There’s no chat, no channels and no tasks.

  • Presence with a bit more nuance. Present, Do Not Disturb, Be Back Later, Offline and On Vacation, each a keyboard shortcut away.
  • A status in a few keystrokes. Press ⌘S, type, hit return. Emoji welcome.
  • Where and when. Everyone’s location and local time, so you can see it’s seven in the morning for someone before you ask them anything.
  • It notices when you’ve gone. If Chicken hasn’t heard from you for five minutes, it marks you as away; after twelve hours, offline. Otherwise the list fills up with people who look present but went to bed hours ago.

Prototyping by using it

The first commit went in at the end of May 2023, and by July the team was using it every day. That’s the part I think matters most. Very little of what Chicken became was planned up front; most of it came from living with it and noticing what was missing.

  • The design came from another prototype. Matthew Lettini had been sketching his own version of the idea, and in July we brought his designs across wholesale, rather than arguing about them in the abstract.
  • Some people live in Slack. Rather than asking them to move, Chicken learned to sync statuses with Slack in both directions. A /st command let you post from Slack too, with shorthand for presence, so /st bbl lunch set you to Be Back Later and /st gnight took you offline.
  • Everyone was in a different place. Locations and local times went in after a few weeks of working out what time it was for each other.
  • Sometimes you only want a glance. So there’s an extremely compact view, small enough to tuck into the corner of a screen.
  • Sharing should go both ways. Emoji reactions on statuses, and notifications when someone arrives, leaves, or reacts to yours.
  • Does it want to be its own window? The cheapest way to find out was a tiny Mac app: a SwiftUI window wrapped around the web app, an evening’s work rather than a real native client.

Arun Srinivasan sanded down a lot of rough edges along the way, especially in how the keyboard shortcuts behaved. In August, we asked a few other remote teams to try it with us.

Where it ended up

Chicken never had a public release, and its last commit went in in December 2023. I don’t think of that as a failure. A prototype’s job is to make a question concrete enough that you can live with it for a while, and Chicken did that: it gave us six months of actually checking in with each other, and a much clearer idea of what “ambient” means for a team that never shares a room.

It’s also a fair picture of how we like to work: start with something small and real, use it every day, and let what you notice decide what comes next. If you’ve got a question like that you’d like to explore, we’d love to hear about it.
